decisions.decision: Tech stack: FastAPI (Python 3.11) backend + Next.js 14 (React + TypeScript, App Router) frontend + PostgreSQL 16 + Docker Compose (local) with portability to any cloud container runtime. SQLAlchemy 2.x ORM + Alembic for migrations.
decisions.rationale: PO-confirmed selection. FastAPI fits well because: (a) the LLD's stock-ledger logic, monthly carry-forward, and SUM/GROUP BY reporting map cleanly to Python services + SQLAlchemy with row-level locking; (b) Pydantic models give us cheap input validation matching the PRD's strict server-side date and integer rules; (c) ASES default stack reduces ramp-up. PostgreSQL chosen over MySQL (LLD open item #1) for stronger transactional guarantees, native row-level locking, and richer date/time types needed for monthly carry-forward.
decisions.tradeoffs: Two-runtime stack (Python + Node) means two Docker images and dependency sets. Acceptable for the scale; simplifies clean separation of concerns and keeps frontend developer experience first-class via Next.js.
alternatives_considered: Next.js API routes only with Prisma: rejected — harder to enforce service-layer separation that the ASES critique lenses check for; mixing frontend and DB logic in one process makes domain testing harder.
Node.js + Express/Nest: rejected — same-language stack but no ASES skill template tuned for it; would also lose the strong Python testing ecosystem for the stock-math domain.

decisions.decision: All writes to tbl_stock_ledger acquire SELECT FOR UPDATE on the latest ledger row for the affected (design_id, grade_id) before computing the new running_balance. The lock is held within the same SQLAlchemy DB transaction that persists the triggering Inward / Sales / Adjustment header + lines.
decisions.rationale: LLD open item #5 explicitly flags concurrent-entry handling. Without serialization, two simultaneous form saves on the same (design, grade) can both read the same prior running balance and write conflicting new balances, corrupting the ledger. SELECT FOR UPDATE is the simplest correct primitive in PostgreSQL and runs entirely server-side without app-level coordination.
decisions.tradeoffs: Transactions involving the same (design, grade) are serialized — at single-factory concurrency this is invisible. If contention ever becomes visible (e.g. dozens of concurrent users on a hot design), revisit with an INSERT-only ledger + on-the-fly running balance read pattern.
alternatives_considered: Optimistic locking with a version column: rejected — requires client retry logic and complicates the form save UX.
Application-level mutex: rejected — does not survive multi-process deployment (multiple uvicorn workers).
Insert-only ledger with computed-on-read running balance: rejected for V1 — pushes computation to the dashboard path where it directly affects user-perceived latency.

decisions.decision: Stock balances are stored materially in tbl_stock_ledger as a running_balance column per write, not computed live via SUM(inward) - SUM(sales) +/- SUM(adjust) on every dashboard read.
decisions.rationale: LLD open item #3 recommends a materialised table over a real-time computed view. Dashboard performance must be sub-second (PRD AC-045). A live SUM grows linearly with transaction count and becomes slow within months. Storing the running balance per write makes every dashboard query an O(1) lookup of the latest row <= as_of_date per (design, grade), at the cost of writing one extra row per form save — a clearly favourable tradeoff at this scale.
decisions.tradeoffs: Back-dated transactions in the 7-day window require recomputing running_balance for all later rows in the same (design, grade). This recomputation runs inside the same DB transaction and is bounded (≤ ~30 rows for a 7-day backdate at realistic throughput).
alternatives_considered: Live SUM in a SQL view: rejected — fails AC-045 at scale.
PostgreSQL MATERIALIZED VIEW with periodic refresh: rejected — stale data between refresh cycles violates dashboard correctness expectations.

decisions.decision: Monthly carry-forward (Opening Balance of Month N+1 = Closing Balance of Month N) is implemented as a deterministic on-read lookup of the previous month's last-day closing balance from tbl_stock_ledger — NOT as a scheduled job that materialises an explicit opening_balance row on the 1st of each month.
decisions.rationale: The data needed for FORMULA-002 is already present in tbl_stock_ledger (every write stores running_balance with txn_date). A simple query 'SELECT running_balance FROM tbl_stock_ledger WHERE design_id=X AND grade_id=G AND txn_date <= LAST_DAY_PREV_MONTH ORDER BY txn_date DESC LIMIT 1' returns the opening balance for the new month with no scheduled job, no time-zone risks, and no failure modes around missed runs. Back-dated transactions are naturally handled because the lookup always reads the current state of the ledger.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slightly more complex dashboard query than reading an explicit opening_balance column — but eliminates an entire class of scheduled-job failure modes (missed runs, partial completions, time-zone bugs).
alternatives_considered: APScheduler job that writes an opening_balance row at 00:00:00 on the 1st of each month: rejected — adds a scheduler dependency, has misfire risk if the server is down at midnight, and creates a sync gap with back-dated transactions.
Storing the opening balance in tbl_stock_ledger as a synthetic 'opening' row on first write of a month: rejected — adds write-path complexity for marginal read-path benefit.

decisions.decision: V1 ships with no authentication and no RBAC. All API endpoints are open and all UI pages are reachable without login. Deployment is restricted to a trusted internal network.
decisions.rationale: Explicit V1 non-goal per HLD §2.2 of the uploaded requirements doc. Adding auth would add ~30% to V1 scope and is being intentionally deferred to V2. Documenting this loud-and-clear as an ADR prevents downstream agents (critic, final-audit) from flagging missing auth as a defect.
decisions.tradeoffs: Anyone with network access can submit transactions. Mitigation: README explicitly calls out V1 limitation; deployment guidance requires trusted internal network; V2 plan reserves an Auth module slot that will wrap existing endpoints with FastAPI dependency-injection auth.
alternatives_considered: Ship V1 with basic HTTP auth: rejected — half-measure that creates a false sense of security and still requires reworking when V2 RBAC arrives.
Delay V1 launch until auth is in: rejected by PO — the business needs the trading-tiles flow operational on the internal network now.

decisions.decision: Frontend (Next.js) and backend (FastAPI) ship as two separate Docker images orchestrated via docker-compose for local development. The frontend image runs in standalone Next.js mode and calls the backend via a public HTTP API; backend never serves the frontend.
decisions.rationale: Clean separation keeps the deployment portable to any cloud (Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run, App Service) where the two tiers may scale independently. Matches the ASES execution-vs-UI agent separation (rule 6 — execution agent never touches UI scaffold; UI agent only touches integration_points).
decisions.tradeoffs: Local dev requires two containers up; CORS must be configured. Both are negligible for the project's complexity.
alternatives_considered: Bundled single image (uvicorn serving Next.js static export): rejected — couples the two tiers and complicates separate scaling and the ASES UI-vs-execution agent contract.
Vercel-hosted frontend + Render-hosted backend: rejected for V1 — adds two SaaS dependencies before the product has validated demand.

decisions.decision: Backend uses a strict four-layer architecture — presentation (FastAPI routers + Pydantic schemas) / application (services) / domain (pure functions + exception types) / infrastructure (SQLAlchemy ORM, repositories, Alembic, config). Each layer may depend only on layers below it. Routers MUST go through services; services MUST go through repositories; no router-to-repository shortcuts.
decisions.rationale: The HLD already prescribes a layered structure (M-003 is domain; M-001/M-004/M-005 are application; M-006 is presentation). Enforcing the boundary at the file-tree level keeps the stock-ledger domain math (S2/S3) testable in isolation and matches what the ASES critique lenses check for (lens 1: contract integrity, lens 4: layering). It also gives /ases-tasks an unambiguous file-owner per concern.
decisions.tradeoffs: More files in S1 than a flat structure — each entity grows from one file to ~3 (model, repository, service, router, schema). Accepted because S1 sets the pattern that S2/S3 will follow; cost amortises.
alternatives_considered: Flat structure (everything under src/): rejected — would force S2 to refactor when stock-ledger domain logic arrives.
Hexagonal/ports-and-adapters with explicit Protocol interfaces: rejected for V1 — adds ceremony without a concrete second adapter to justify it. Revisit if/when we add a second persistence backend.

decisions.decision: All 6 master entities in V1 are soft-delete only. HTTP DELETE /<entity>/{id} sets is_active=false and returns the deactivated row; there is no hard-delete endpoint. The repository BaseRepository exposes soft_delete() — there is no delete() method.
decisions.rationale: Every master's acceptance criteria explicitly require soft delete (AC-002 supplier, AC-005 staff, AC-008 dealer, AC-012 grade, AC-015 design, AC-017 design-grade-map). Forbidding hard delete at the repository level prevents accidental data loss when transaction data exists for the deactivated master (HLD R-005). Mapping the standard DELETE verb to a soft delete keeps the REST surface conventional while encoding the V1 invariant.
decisions.tradeoffs: Cannot delete genuinely erroneous rows. Mitigation: admin can rename them (PATCH) and deactivate. If true purge becomes necessary in V2, an explicit POST /<entity>/{id}/purge endpoint will be added with stronger guardrails.
alternatives_considered: Separate DELETE (hard) + PATCH is_active (soft): rejected — gives admins a hard-delete footgun for V1.
Disable DELETE entirely and require explicit PATCH is_active=false: rejected — less intuitive than the conventional verb mapping; admin UI would need a custom action.

decisions.decision: Alembic migrations are generated via `alembic revision --autogenerate` with the SQLAlchemy ORM models as the single source of truth (target_metadata = Base.metadata). Hand-written SQL migrations are forbidden for schema DDL in V1; only data-only operations (back-fills) may be hand-written.
decisions.rationale: ORM-first keeps the model and migration in lock-step automatically. The baseline placeholder 0001_baseline.sql will be replaced by 0002_master_tables.py generated from the ORM. Reviewer verifies the generated DDL against the LLD column spec before commit.
decisions.tradeoffs: Autogenerate has known blind spots (CHECK constraints, partial indexes). Mitigated by reviewing every generated migration against the LLD and adding op.create_check_constraint / op.create_index lines by hand where autogenerate misses them.
alternatives_considered: Hand-written SQL migrations: rejected — duplicates the schema in two places, drifts inevitably.
ORM-only, no Alembic, use SQLAlchemy create_all on startup: rejected — fine for dev, breaks any disciplined production deploy.

decisions.decision: All backend HTTP endpoints are versioned under the path prefix /api/v1. The frontend NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL points at http://<host>:8000/api/v1. Breaking schema changes will introduce /api/v2 in parallel with a deprecation window on /api/v1.
decisions.rationale: Establishes the versioning convention before any consumer exists. Cheap to do now; expensive to retrofit when a third-party integration shows up in V2.
decisions.tradeoffs: Every router mount adds a trivial prefix; no real downside.
alternatives_considered: Unversioned (/suppliers, /grades…): rejected — locks the project into single-version mode and forces a forklift when versioning becomes necessary.
Header-based versioning (Accept: application/vnd.jayanth.v1+json): rejected — over-engineered for an internal V1 with a single frontend.

decisions.decision: Admin forms are composed from react-hook-form + Zod resolver + shadcn primitives (Label, Input, Select). The shadcn `form.tsx` shim is NOT introduced. Per-entity form components live under frontend/src/components/admin/<entity>/<Entity>Form.tsx.
decisions.rationale: Closes TD-002 from /ases-scaffold. The shadcn radix-nova preset has no `form.tsx` registry entry, and adding a hand-rolled shim now would create maintenance debt the moment shadcn 5.x ships its own. react-hook-form + Zod already covers field-level errors, submit state, and resolver validation — there is no functional gap.
decisions.tradeoffs:
Slightly more boilerplate per form (manual Label+Input pairs and error

tags) than shadcn's Form composer would give. Acceptable for 6 simple forms; revisit if Sprint 2/3 forms balloon.
alternatives_considered: Hand-roll a local form.tsx shim mirroring shadcn 3.x: rejected — duplicates an upstream component that will reappear in a future shadcn release.
Adopt Conform / Formik: rejected — different mental model from react-hook-form, no team familiarity.

decisions.decision: Database access uses a generic BaseRepository[TModel] with list / get / create / update / soft_delete plus per-entity subclasses that add entity-specific finders. Services depend on repositories — they never construct queries directly.
decisions.rationale: Six master entities share identical CRUD shapes. A generic base eliminates ~150 lines of duplication and gives the test suite a single seam to mock for unit tests of services. Per-entity finders (e.g. GradeRepository.get_by_code, DesignGradeMapRepository.list_active_by_design) extend the base without breaking the contract.
decisions.tradeoffs: Generic typing in Python (TypeVar + __class_getitem__) is slightly less ergonomic than per-entity hand-written CRUD. Accepted because the per-entity boilerplate cost across 6 entities far exceeds the one-time generic-setup cost.
alternatives_considered: Per-entity hand-written CRUD: rejected — 6x duplication, harder to enforce DS-008 soft-delete invariant.
Raw SQLAlchemy in services (no repository layer): rejected — couples services to ORM concerns and breaks DS-007 layering.

decisions.decision: Denormalize `place` onto tbl_inward_header.place and tbl_sales_header.place — snapshotted from tbl_supplier_master / tbl_dealer_master at form-save time. Master-place edits do NOT propagate retroactively to historical transactions. The S1 admin route to edit a supplier's or dealer's place remains; it just doesn't backfill.
decisions.rationale: PRD AC-022 / AC-029 specify place is auto-populated from the master and rendered read-only at form time — but the PRD is silent on whether the form snapshots the value or the saved transaction joins back to the master on read. Snapshotting gives (a) historically stable reads (a transaction from 2026-03-01 keeps the supplier's place as it was on 2026-03-01 even if the master is edited later), and (b) one fewer JOIN on S3's Sales Report (M-005) hot path. Both align with the PRD's framing of transactions as an immutable historical record.
decisions.tradeoffs: Master-place edits aren't reflected in historical transactions — but this is the desired semantic for an accounting/ledger system, not a bug. Storage cost is a Text column per row; negligible at the project's scale.
alternatives_considered: JOIN at read time: rejected — forfeits historical immutability; if a supplier moves cities post-transaction, last year's purchase records would silently show the new city.
Snapshot + audit table tracking edits to the master: rejected — overkill for V1; PRD does not require an audit trail.

decisions.decision: Close TD-007 in S2 by upgrading TimestampMixin to emit TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (DateTime(timezone=True)) at the ORM level; the S2 migration 0003 also ALTERs the 4 existing S1 created_at columns (tbl_supplier_master, tbl_staff_master, tbl_dealer_master, tbl_trading_design_master) from TIMESTAMP to TIMESTAMPTZ in one shot. All 7 new S2 tables land with TIMESTAMPTZ from the start.
decisions.rationale: TD-007 was filed in S1 final-audit when the LLD prose (TIMESTAMPTZ) drifted from the ORM (plain DateTime). S2 introduces 7 new tables — landing them with TIMESTAMPTZ avoids re-spawning the same drift, and altering the S1 columns at the same time keeps the schema uniform. PostgreSQL's ALTER COLUMN TYPE TIMESTAMPTZ from TIMESTAMP is data-preserving and effectively instant at our row counts. The TimestampMixin is the single source of truth, so a one-line ORM change cascades into all 11 tables consistently. Per DS-009 (ORM-first), the ORM change drives the migration.
decisions.tradeoffs: One-time ALTER on 4 S1 tables. Acceptable because (a) created_at is server-default-only — no application code writes it, (b) ALTER COLUMN TYPE is fast at our row counts (millions or less), (c) the alternative (split-policy ORM with two mixins) creates a maintenance trap where every new table risks regressing.
alternatives_considered: Split policy — new TimestampMixinTZ mixin for S2+ tables only: rejected — schema becomes inconsistent, and developers must remember which mixin to use.
Defer TD-007 indefinitely: rejected — every new table introduced post-S1 would compound the drift.
Drop created_at entirely on transaction tables: rejected — accounting/ledger systems need a created_at for audit; PRD AC chain implies it.

decisions.decision: Amend DS-002 wording: serialization for stock_ledger writes per (design, grade) MUST acquire pg_advisory_xact_lock(design_id, grade_id) BEFORE the SELECT ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE on the latest row. The FOR UPDATE row lock alone is INSUFFICIENT because PostgreSQL's SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE does not re-resolve LIMIT after waiting on a row lock — the waiter re-reads the originally-identified row, missing the row just inserted by the holder. Discovered + fixed in S2 via TD-011 (advisory lock added to domain.stock._apply). This decision documents the layered pattern so future write paths don't regress.
decisions.rationale: Closes FA-S2-002/003 and RI-003 from S2 final-audit. DS-002's original text described only the FOR UPDATE primitive; the verified safe implementation requires advisory-lock-first. Spec text must catch up to implementation reality.
decisions.tradeoffs: Advisory lock adds ~1 RTT per write call (negligible). Spec is now more prescriptive about the lock pattern — future contributors implementing a new write path on the ledger must compose both locks; if they only do FOR UPDATE, they recreate TD-011.
alternatives_considered: Replace FOR UPDATE with advisory lock alone: rejected — FOR UPDATE provides row-visibility guarantees (the read returns latest committed within the lock) that advisory locks alone don't. Keep both for defense-in-depth.
Switch isolation level to SERIALIZABLE with retry: rejected — adds retry complexity to every write path; advisory lock is simpler.
Lock the (design, grade) row in tbl_design_grade_map as the sentinel: rejected — that table is read-mostly and locking it on every ledger write couples concurrent admin edits to all writers.

decisions.decision: Stock Dashboard aggregation uses a SINGLE GROUP BY query with CASE-conditional SUMs (over tbl_stock_ledger filtered by date range), NOT per-(design, grade) sub-queries. Opening + Closing per row remain O(1) latest_as_of lookups against the materialized running_balance per DS-003/004.
decisions.rationale: Dashboard target is sub-second (PRD AC-045). Per-(design, grade) sub-queries would be O(N) where N is active pair count (initially ~6, scaling with design+grade growth) — slow with full table scan per sub-query. The single GROUP BY uses ix_stock_ledger_dgt's (design_id, grade_id) prefix + the txn_date range to scan only the in-window rows once. Opening/Closing remain index-O(1) per pair.
decisions.tradeoffs: Single CASE-aggregated SQL is slightly less readable than 4 separate small queries. Acceptable — the SQL is a stable, well-commented expression in LedgerAggregatesRepository.
alternatives_considered: Per-pair sub-queries (4 sub-queries × N pairs): rejected — at PRD scale of 12 months × O(1000) txns this can exceed sub-second target.
Pre-aggregated monthly summary table: rejected — adds a maintenance path (refresh-on-write) and the savings are speculative for V1 volumes.
Materialized view refreshed on each transaction: rejected — same maintenance burden plus stale-window risk.

decisions.decision: Sales Report consolidation + transactions queries share a SINGLE filter predicate construction function (built once per request, applied to both queries). This guarantees AC-050 reconciliation (sum(transactions.nos) == sum(consolidation.total_nos)) by construction — divergent filter logic between the two queries is impossible.
decisions.rationale: AC-050 is a critical correctness invariant for the dual-payload report. Hand-maintaining matching filter clauses across two SELECT statements is fragile; a shared predicate-builder enforces parity by construction.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slightly more code structure (helper function) for what could otherwise be two inline WHEREs. Negligible cost.
alternatives_considered: Inline two separate filter clauses: rejected — AC-050 violations would be silent until tested.
Run a single query and post-aggregate in Python: rejected — pushes work out of Postgres into Python where it's slower and harder to test.

decisions.decision: Authentication uses JWT (JSON Web Tokens) signed with HS256 via python-jose, with an 8-hour access token TTL. Credentials are stored as bcrypt hashes via passlib. No refresh tokens in V2. FastAPI OAuth2PasswordBearer extracts the Bearer token from the Authorization header. get_current_user re-fetches is_active from the DB on every request so deactivation takes effect immediately.
decisions.rationale: JWT is stateless — no session store required, compatible with the existing single-process uvicorn deployment. 8-hour TTL matches a typical trading day, minimising re-login friction. Bcrypt is the industry standard for password hashing. python-jose + passlib are the canonical FastAPI auth stack. Refresh tokens add storage and rotation complexity with marginal benefit at single-tenant single-site scale.
decisions.tradeoffs: No token revocation in V2 — a deactivated user's existing token remains valid until expiry (up to 8h). Mitigated by DB is_active re-check on every request — deactivation takes effect on the next API call, not at token expiry.
alternatives_considered: Session-based auth (server-side sessions): rejected — requires a session store (Redis or DB table), adds infrastructure dependency.
Short TTL (1h) + refresh tokens: rejected — adds client-side token rotation complexity; overkill for V2 internal-network use.
API key per user: rejected — no per-request expiry, harder to revoke, no standard FastAPI integration.

decisions.decision: RBAC uses a single role enum column on tbl_user_master — three roles: STAFF (data entry + read reports), VERIFIER (read only: dashboard + reports), SUPERVISOR (full access including user + price + invoice management). No separate roles or permissions tables.
decisions.rationale: Three fixed roles map directly to PRD user types (Data Entry Staff, Stock Verifier, Management/Supervisor). A roles table with many-to-many user↔role adds 3+ tables and a join on every request for a system with exactly 3 roles. The enum column is O(1) to check — role is embedded in the JWT payload, no extra DB query needed for role checks. Role expansion beyond 3 would warrant a permissions table; V2 scope does not require it.
decisions.tradeoffs: Role enum is a schema migration if a 4th role is added. Acceptable — migrations are cheap and the ORM change is one field.
alternatives_considered: Separate tbl_role + tbl_user_role many-to-many: rejected — 2 extra tables, FK joins, and migration complexity for 3 roles that won't change in V2.
Permission bitfield per user: rejected — opaque, hard to audit, not readable by non-developers.

decisions.decision: TD-008 (first-row insert race in tbl_stock_ledger when no prior row exists for a (design, grade) pair) is CLOSED by DS-015's pg_advisory_xact_lock. No code change to domain/stock.py required. V2 adds a new integration test TC covering the concurrent first-row insert scenario for explicit regression coverage.
decisions.rationale: The pg_advisory_xact_lock(design_id, grade_id) mandated by DS-015 is a transaction-level exclusive lock. When two sessions both call it for the same (design, grade), the second blocks until the first commits — including the first-row case. The domain.stock._apply function in backend/src/domain/stock.py already implements this (TD-011 closed in S2). The gap was test coverage — TC-087 (S2) assumed a pre-existing row. V2 closes that gap with a test.
decisions.tradeoffs: Test-only addition — zero risk of regression. The advisory lock was live in production at V1 ship.
alternatives_considered: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (upsert): considered — would also handle first-row, but changes the ledger's append-only semantics and complicates running_balance recomputation.
Lock the design_grade_map row as sentinel: rejected by DS-015 — couples admin edits to ledger write path.

decisions.decision: Report export uses reportlab for PDF generation and openpyxl for Excel (XLSX) generation. Both produce BytesIO objects returned via FastAPI StreamingResponse.
decisions.rationale: reportlab: mature Python PDF library, pure Python, no external binary dependencies (unlike wkhtmltopdf or weasyprint), generates tabular reports via SimpleDocTemplate + Table without HTML intermediary. openpyxl: pure Python XLSX writer, MIT licence, no LibreOffice/Java dependency, well-maintained, produces native .xlsx that Excel and Google Sheets open natively. StreamingResponse avoids buffering large files fully in memory before sending.
decisions.tradeoffs: reportlab's API is verbose — building tables requires explicit column widths and styles. Acceptable for 2 report types with stable layouts.
alternatives_considered: weasyprint (HTML→PDF): rejected — requires libpango/libcairo system libraries, complicating the Docker image.
xlsxwriter (Excel): rejected — write-only, no read capability if ever needed; openpyxl is more broadly useful.
pandas.DataFrame.to_excel: rejected — pulls in pandas as a dependency for a use-case that doesn't need DataFrame semantics.

decisions.decision: Active price for invoice line population = the tbl_price_master row WHERE design_id=X AND grade_id=G AND is_active=True AND effective_from <= invoice_date ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1. unit_price is snapshotted onto tbl_invoice_line at invoice creation time (immutable after creation). If no active price exists for a (design, grade), unit_price=0 is used and the line carries a warning note.
decisions.rationale: Effective-from price lookup gives time-aware pricing: a price change introduced later doesn't affect invoices generated before that date. Snapshotting unit_price on invoice creation follows DS-013 (place denormalisation) — immutable historical invoices. Zero-price fallback prevents invoice creation from blocking when prices are not yet configured, matching the PO's workflow where prices may be back-filled after sales entry.
decisions.tradeoffs: A zero-price invoice line is a warning state, not an error. Admin must notice and re-invoice if needed. Alternative (block on missing price) was rejected because it couples invoice creation to price configuration completeness.
alternatives_considered: Block invoice if price missing: rejected — prevents invoicing newly introduced design-grade combinations during a price-configuration catch-up window.
Use latest active price regardless of effective_from: rejected — removes time-aware pricing capability.
Store price as FK reference on invoice_line: rejected — allows retroactive price edits to silently change historical invoice amounts.

decisions.decision: Invoices are created on-demand by SUPERVISOR via POST /invoices {sales_header_id} — NOT auto-triggered during sales saves. One invoice per sales transaction enforced by UNIQUE(sales_header_id) on tbl_invoice_header. invoice_number is deterministic: 'INV-{YYYYMMDD}-{sales_header_id:05d}'.
decisions.rationale: Auto-triggering invoice creation on every POST /sales would require prices to be configured for all (design, grade) pairs before any sale can be saved — blocking the data-entry flow that was operational in V1. On-demand creation gives the supervisor control over the invoicing timeline and accommodates the common scenario where prices are configured after sales are entered. The UNIQUE constraint prevents double-invoicing. Deterministic invoice_number means accidental duplicate creation attempts get a clean 409.
decisions.tradeoffs: Invoices must be created manually per sale — a supervisor could forget to invoice some transactions. Mitigation: GET /invoices can be enhanced in V3 to filter by uninvoiced sales (LEFT JOIN on sales_header_id IS NULL). V2 does not include this endpoint.
alternatives_considered: Auto-create invoice in sales save transaction: rejected — blocks sales entry when prices are missing; tight coupling between M-002 (transactions) and M-011 (invoicing).
Batch invoice creation (invoice all un-invoiced sales): considered for V3 — useful but out of V2 scope.

decisions.decision: V2 auth login wire format is OAuth2 form-encoded (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), NOT JSON. The router POST /auth/login binds `form: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()` per RFC 6749 §4.3.2 and DS-018's OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl='/api/v1/auth/login'). TC-208/TC-209 body field is a semantic payload description (which fields are sent: username, password), NOT a wire-format directive — Phase 3 test-impl will encode via httpx `data=` (form-encoded), not `json=`. LLD line 236 (`data: LoginRequest`) is documentation drift and will be corrected in the next LLD refresh.
decisions.rationale: Resolves the residual documentation-drift flagged by T-072 iter3 critique (findings F-T072-01 RESOLVED_BY_REINTERPRETATION). Under ASES Hard Rule 2 (plan.json is authoritative), the router correctly implements the form-encoded contract. Making this explicit as an ADR prevents Phase 3 test-impl from mistakenly encoding TC bodies as JSON, and prevents future contributors from 'fixing' the router to accept JSON in a misguided attempt to match LLD prose.
decisions.tradeoffs: TC-208/209 bodies read as JSON on a naive glance — reviewers must recall this ADR when reading V2 auth test cases. Alternative (rewrite the router to accept JSON at /auth/login) rejected because it breaks OAuth2 spec compliance and Swagger 'Authorize' flow.
alternatives_considered: Introduce a JSON login endpoint alongside the form-encoded one: rejected — two endpoints for the same action, doubles the auth surface, and Swagger 'Authorize' only supports the OAuth2 form-encoded contract.
Rewrite router to accept LoginRequest (JSON body): rejected — breaks OAuth2PasswordBearer semantics and RFC 6749 conformance.

decisions.decision: V2 non-auth routers (users, prices, invoices, reports/inward, reports/export) rely on route-level `Depends(get_current_user)` declared inside each router file, NOT on mount-level `dependencies=[Depends(get_current_user)]` on the `app.include_router(...)` call in main.py. Only the 11 V1 routers carry the mount-level dependency (added by T-092). auth_router is mounted with no dependency at all (open endpoint per DS-018). This deviation from LLD prose is intentional and documented inline on main.py:64 and 68-69.
decisions.rationale: FastAPI dedupes identical Depends within a single request, so the two patterns are behaviorally equivalent. The V2 as-built pattern keeps each router file self-contained for auth semantics (a reader of routers/users.py sees the guard at each route), whereas mount-level deps hide the requirement from anyone reading the router in isolation. T-092 iter3 F-092-4 accepted this as an is_adr_tradeoff. TC-213 (auth-guard regression across V1 mounts) is unaffected.
decisions.tradeoffs: LLD prose says 'apply auth dep globally via mount-level dependencies=[...]' — as-built deviates. LLD prose will be refreshed at next LLD update. Cost: reviewers must know both patterns coexist (V1 mount-level for legacy, V2 route-level for new). Benefit: V2 router files are self-documenting for auth requirements.
alternatives_considered: Refactor all V2 routers to remove route-level Depends and add mount-level dep in main.py: rejected — behavior unchanged, cost is real code churn across 5 router files with zero test impact.

Also strip route-level Depends from V1 routers to match V2: rejected — V1 auth guard is currently mount-level for a reason (T-092 kept V1 mount-level to minimize touch surface); LLD refresh will pick one direction.
